stories.headline: B.C. First Nations go to court over Pacific Link’s ‘national interest’ designation
stories.deck: Several First Nations, including the St’át’imc Chiefs Council, filed federal judicial reviews seeking to overturn Ottawa’s decision to list the Alberta-to-B.C. oil pipeline as a project of national interest under the Building Canada Act.
stories.summary: Several First Nations, including the St’át’imc Chiefs Council representing 11 communities, filed federal judicial reviews seeking to overturn Ottawa’s decision to list the Pacific Link oil pipeline as a project of national interest under the Building Canada Act, CBC News reported Monday. The proposed line would move about one million barrels a day from Bruderheim, Alta., to a deepwater port near Delta, B.C. Listing shifts the federal focus from whether to build to how, by fast-tracking approvals. The nations argue the listing “effectively acts as an approval” and that duty-to-consult obligations must be met before a project is listed. Chief Bonnie Adolph said her community was refused consultation because its territory is not directly on the route, despite Fraser River watershed concerns. Other applicants include Boston Bar, Cheam, Lower Nicola, Kwantlen, Kwikwetlem, Skeetchestn and Tsartlip, plus Cold Lake First Nations in Alberta. Pacific Link said Indigenous participation, including possible equity ownership, is central to the project. CBC said it had sought a federal response.
stories.why: A court fight over consultation could slow one of the Carney government’s marquee energy projects.
stories.label: Reported + allegation
stories.note: The nations’ claim that Canada breached its duty to consult is their court argument, not a finding.

stories.deck: The 20-year-old Mercedes driver sealed the title with third place behind Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton, breaking Sebastian Vettel’s age record and becoming Italy’s first champion since 1953.
stories.summary: Kimi Antonelli sealed his first Formula 1 world title at 20 years and 68 days by finishing third at the Mexico City Grand Prix, BBC Sport and Reuters/Al Jazeera reported. stories.headline: Supreme Court turns down Trump administration's bid to make California set aside about 20,000 disputed mail ballots
stories.deck: On the eve of the midterms, the Supreme Court denied the Justice Department's emergency request to make California keep separate the mail ballots of more than 20,000 people the administration says are likely noncitizens. Lower courts had already refused.
stories.summary: On the eve of the midterms, the Supreme Court denied the Justice Department's emergency request to make California keep separate the mail ballots of more than 20,000 people the administration says are likely noncitizens. Lower courts had already refused. The department had sent California's secretary of state and Los Angeles County's top election official a list of about 20,000 registered voters it says are not citizens, and asked that their ballots be held back until citizenship could be verified. State and county officials questioned the list's accuracy and warned that eligible voters could be disenfranchised. On Oct 28, U.S. District Judge David Carter refused a temporary order, writing that voters must not lose a core right 'because of unfounded allegations stemming from a procedure rife with uncertainty and errors'. A divided 9th Circuit panel (2-1) also refused on Friday, Oct 30. Solicitor General D. John Sauer then asked the justices on Monday morning to order the ballots kept apart, arguing that once they are mixed in 'there is no way to get the challenged ballots back'. NPR and AP reported Monday evening that the court had denied the request.
stories.why: California has more than 23 million registered voters and had received over 6 million mail ballots by Sunday, CBS News reported. The ruling means ballots are processed under the state's normal rules while the underlying lawsuit continues.
stories.label: Reported + allegation
stories.note: As of our check, the Supreme Court's online docket listed only the application (filed Nov 2), not the order, and we had not seen the order's text, so we can't say whether any justices dissented. The noncitizen accusation is the administration's and has not been proven in court.

He acknowledged that a sitting president's party usually loses midterms, adding: 'But we gave this a very strong shot.' CBS News, citing the University of Florida Voting Lab, says more than 57 million Americans had voted early.
stories.why: It's the president's final public argument before polls open Tuesday, Nov 3. His remark about midterm history is being read as preparing for possible Republican losses; the results will show how much it mattered.
stories.label: Reported + claim
stories.note: The vandalism explanation and the $5,000 promise are Trump's claims; the first is disputed by his own U.S. attorney's court statement, per CNBC.

stories.headline: Belgian PM Bart De Wever offers his resignation after budget talks collapse; the king holds off
stories.summary: De Wever went to the palace Monday after his five-party 'Arizona' coalition failed overnight to agree how to find about €10 billion in savings for 2027. King Philippe took the resignation 'under consideration', will consult coalition party leaders from Tuesday and meets De Wever again Friday, urging compromise. The split is left-right: Vooruit, CD&V and Les Engagés want more from higher earners; N-VA and MR want spending cuts. Belgium's deficit was 5% of GDP last year, above the EU's 3% limit.
stories.why: A government collapse could mean emergency monthly budgets or new elections in a country that hosts the EU and NATO.
stories.label: Reported
stories.note: What happens if the king accepts is unclear: Euronews says new elections would follow; VRT says a new majority could in principle be formed without them.

stories.headline: Russia resumes strikes on Kherson after the war's longest truce ends; alert apps hacked on both sides
stories.summary: A local ceasefire in Ukraine's Kherson region that let hundreds of people leave Russian-occupied Oleshky ended Sunday night; a Ukrainian official told AFP Russia refused to extend it. On Monday morning a Russian drone hit a car in Kherson's Korabelny district, wounding two older residents, local authorities said. Ukraine's air-alert app sent fake radiation warnings Sunday night, and Russia said its emergency-warning app suffered a 'massive cyberattack' on Monday. US-mediated talks are due to resume this month.
stories.why: The truce was the only real pause in fighting in the full-scale war; its end leaves civilians exposed again as winter power cuts deepen.
stories.label: Reported + allegation
stories.note: Ongoing: the Oleshky evacuations were in Edition 1 (Nov 1). Claims about who attacked the apps are unverified.

stories.headline: Kimi Antonelli, 20, becomes F1's youngest world champion as Verstappen wins in Mexico City
stories.summary: Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli clinched the 2026 title by finishing third at the Mexico City Grand Prix, at 20 years and 68 days, breaking Sebastian Vettel's record (23 in 2010). He is the first Italian champion since Alberto Ascari in 1953. Max Verstappen won from fifth on the grid, holding off Lewis Hamilton by 0.8 seconds in a race with a red flag after Valtteri Bottas crashed (he got out unaided) and a late safety car. The season continues in São Paulo on Nov. 6–8.
stories.why: It is a new age record for the sport and Italy's first drivers' title in 73 years, with races still to run.
stories.label: Reported

stories.headline: Michigan Democrat Haley Stevens endorses Republican Mike Rogers for Senate, two days before the vote
stories.summary: Rep. Haley Stevens, who lost the Democratic primary to Abdul El-Sayed, appeared with GOP nominee Mike Rogers at a Detroit church on Sunday and then endorsed him in a video. She said El-Sayed had told her she was no longer welcome at his events. She has criticized him over his past campaigning with streamer Hasan Piker and over an ad by Cenk Uygur blaming Israel for high grocery prices; El-Sayed's campaign says it had nothing to do with the ad and criticized it. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called the move a "despicable betrayal"; El-Sayed told reporters it doesn't matter to voters. Trump praised her at his Iowa rally.
stories.why: Michigan's open seat is one of the races that decides whether Democrats can win the Senate, and the split exposes a wider Democratic rift over Israel.
stories.label: Fact

stories.headline: Judge throws out DOJ bid to set aside 'second Dan Sullivan' ballots in Alaska; DOJ appeals
stories.summary: U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason on Sunday dismissed the Justice Department's lawsuit seeking to separate ballots cast for little-known candidate Daniel J. Sullivan and to hold off certifying the Senate race if Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan loses. She wrote that the request would violate Alaskans' right to a secret ballot. The department said it will appeal. Republicans allege Democrat Mary Peltola's camp recruited the second Sullivan to confuse voters; Peltola denies it. Separately, California Gov. Gavin Newsom on Oct 31 wrote to the state's four chief federal judges warning they may be asked for warrants to seize ballots before results are certified.
stories.why: Courts are now refereeing how votes are counted and certified in races that could decide control of Congress.
stories.label: Fact + allegation
stories.note: Ongoing: an earlier ruling against DOJ pressure on election officials was in Edition 1 (Nov 1).

stories.headline: Trump closes the campaign in Iowa and Kansas as GOP defends its majorities
stories.summary: After canceling and then reinstating the in-person stops, Trump rallied Sunday in Dubuque, Iowa, where Republicans are defending a Senate seat, the governorship and a competitive House district, and then headed to Salina, Kansas, where Sen. Roger Marshall faces an unexpectedly close race. Republicans hold the Senate 53-47 and a narrow House edge. More than 52 million Americans had already voted, a midterm record, according to the University of Florida Election Lab.
stories.why: Campaigning in states Trump won easily shows how defensive the GOP has become going into Tuesday's vote.

stories.headline: NYC voters: five city charter questions are on the back of Tuesday's ballot
stories.summary: Besides the races for Congress and state offices, New York City ballots carry five yes-or-no charter amendments from the Commission on Government Efficiency (COGE), the 2026 charter review commission: (1) faster permits for sidewalk cafes, ramps and planters; (2) less contractor paperwork; (3) quicker street-safety projects, sales of unused city property and office leasing, with City Planning Commission approval instead of a Council vote on property sales; (4) a central construction-permit hub at the Buildings Department; and (5) a target for the city's rainy-day reserves. Polls are open 6 a.m. to 9 p.m. on Nov 3.
stories.why: Question 3 in particular would shift some land-sale decisions away from the City Council, so it's worth reading before you vote.

stories.headline: Carney and Trump talk trade; teams to work on a deal 'in the coming weeks'
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney said he had a "good conversation" with Trump and that negotiators will work toward a deal that respects Canada's languages, culture and sovereignty. Trump said there is "the concept of a deal" that would be good for U.S. farmers and "fine for Canada." A senior Canadian source told CBC it is unclear what form the talks will take, and autos are expected to remain a sticking point, as they were when talks collapsed in August.
stories.why: The tariff war hits Canadian jobs in autos, steel and aluminum; any deal, or no deal, shapes prices on both sides of the border.

stories.headline: Alberta's elections chief says: keep the old riding map or delay the 2027 vote
stories.summary: In a letter dated Oct 30, Chief Electoral Officer Gordon McClure told MLAs that Elections Alberta needs 12 to 18 months to run an election on new boundaries and cannot prepare for two maps at once, so the Oct 18, 2027 election should use current boundaries or be postponed. A contested boundary report is due in the legislature Monday. NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi says the proposed map gerrymanders Calgary and Lethbridge and vows a court challenge; Premier Danielle Smith denies manipulating the vote. The justice minister's office says it is reviewing the letter.
stories.why: It raises the prospect of Alberta's next election being delayed amid a fight over fair representation.
stories.label: Fact + allegation

stories.headline: Ottawa quietly shelves the 'Jane Goodall Act' on elephant and great ape captivity
stories.summary: The bill, which would have banned new captivity, breeding and import or export of elephants and great apes except for conservation, welfare or research, passed the Senate in 2024 but died when Parliament was prorogued in January 2025. Despite a 2025 Liberal campaign pledge, the environment minister's office told CBC no decision has been made to reintroduce it. Advocates suspect the government's focus on the tariff war. About 23 elephants live in Canada.
stories.why: Ottawa says zoos and animal welfare are mainly provincial matters, so for now there's no national rule on keeping these animals.
stories.label: Fact + opinion

Amendments are to go to the Legislative Council this year, and Commerce Secretary Algernon Yau hopes they pass by April. stories.summary: Police said undercover officers spent months inside two triad groups that befriended young people in online game chats and billiard halls, held simple initiation rituals, then used them for assaults, intimidation, drug trafficking and money laundering. stories.summary: Lan Kwai Fong Group chairman Allan Zeman said the nightlife district drew 105,000 people on Halloween night, up from 80,000 a year earlier, on the last day of the Tourism Board's first month-long Halloween programme. He said bars and restaurants did roughly double a normal Saturday's business. About half or more of the crowd were locals and 20-30% mainland visitors, by his estimate, with more international tourists than before.

stories.headline: Communist Party publishes plenum resolution tightening oversight of officials and their families
stories.summary: Xinhua released the full resolution on "full and rigorous Party self-governance" adopted at the fifth plenum. It calls for tighter career-long oversight of officials, starting with senior ranks, checks on those whose family assets or spending far exceed their income, closer watch on business activities of officials' spouses and children, and a drive against nepotism. In an accompanying explanation, Xi Jinping said misconduct and "hidden dangers" persist; the SCMP notes he argued strict discipline does not stifle growth.
stories.why: It sets the tone for Party discipline ahead of next year's Party congress, where a leadership reshuffle is expected.
stories.label: Fact (state media)

stories.headline: China and Switzerland sign an upgraded free-trade deal during Swiss president's Beijing visit
stories.summary: Swiss President Guy Parmelin met Xi Jinping, and the two sides signed a protocol upgrading their 2014 free-trade agreement, covering goods, services, investment, digital trade and more. Switzerland says it is the first Chinese trade deal with a legally binding chapter on labour and environmental standards. Both countries must still ratify it. China's commerce ministry put 2025 bilateral trade at $49.04 billion.
stories.why: It is a rare new trade opening between China and a Western economy amid global tariff fights.

stories.summary: At a space symposium in Beijing, program officials said two Long March 10 rockets will separately launch the Lanyue lander and Mengzhou crew ship, which will dock in lunar orbit before two astronauts descend. Before any crewed landing, China plans first flights of both spacecraft and a full uncrewed rehearsal of the mission. China aims to land astronauts this decade; no launch dates were given.

stories.headline: Iliana Yotova wins Bulgaria's presidential runoff to become its first woman president, parallel counts show
stories.summary: Completed parallel counts by polling agencies put acting President Iliana Yotova at about 56.6% to 58.2%, against 38.6% to 40.6% for pro-Western challenger Andrey Gyurov, who conceded. Turnout was below 30%. Yotova, backed by Prime Minister Rumen Radev's governing Progressive Bulgaria, opposes more arms for Ukraine and favors a negotiated peace. Official results were still pending.

stories.summary: The U.S. Embassy warned Saturday of a credible threat of a mass-casualty event at Moscow's Tsaritsyno Museum Reserve, and Canada repeated the alert. Russian media reported the site was closed and evacuated. Russia's FSB said Sunday it verified the U.S. tip and detained a Russian minor who had posted TikTok photos in tactical gear with an object resembling an automatic weapon. stories.headline: Rioting and looting in Frankfurt after Germany's 'Gen Z' protests; 100+ police hurt
stories.summary: Tens of thousands joined largely peaceful 'Gen Z regelt' rallies in German cities on Saturday over school funding, living costs and military conscription. In Frankfurt, rioters later damaged 17 shops and looted five, attacking police with stones, fireworks and petrol bombs. Police arrested 54 people aged 13 to 29; more than 100 officers were injured. Hesse's interior minister said most suspects were German nationals but many had immigrant backgrounds; the city's mayor said passports don't matter, only accountability. Organisers condemned the violence and plan to join Europe-wide protests on Nov 20.
stories.why: It follows riots in France last month, as a youth protest wave spreads across Europe.
